name: Zane Rossi

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hi Zane, thanks for your time. I work for the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or government. What you say here is confidential. Can you start by walking me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Sure. I'm a junior buyer at a building materials distributor, we supply timber, plasterboard, cement and insulation to small builders and a few housing developers. I buy the timber and sheet materials from about a dozen mills and importers. Prices swing every week, so I use AI tools all day to track them, draft orders and compare quotes, and my boss Frank signs off anything big.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Reading the builders. The AI tells me what sold last spring, but Frank knows that when a certain developer goes quiet, a big order is coming. I bought too much decking timber in August because I trusted the numbers, and it's still sitting in the yard.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I live with my girlfriend Lucia, she's a hairdresser at a salon in town. We've got about three months of costs saved, plus a bit I make selling offcuts and damaged sheets online at weekends, maybe three hundred a month. My granddad was a carpenter and he always said, work for yourself if you can. I think about that a lot.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a good tool, nothing more, and anyone who said it would replace everyone was selling something. I'd keep showing the lads at work how I use it. Builders don't care how I find the price, they just want the timber on Tuesday.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'd be pleased, because I'm ahead on the tools and the field stays level. The bigger thing for me is house building slowing down, which affects all our orders. AI or not, a quiet building year is a quiet year for me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going, learn to read the builders better, and use the AI to cut down on mistakes like the decking. I'd grow the offcuts business to maybe six hundred a month. And I'd start saving towards a van, because I want my own trade supply business one day.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Honestly, a bit fired up, because I'd have time to build something.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You want your own business. What would it be?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A small trade supplier for one area, maybe just sheet materials and fixings, delivered same day. The big distributors are slow with small builders. I'd be quick, and I'd know every builder by name.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you tell first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Lucia, she's got her own chair at the salon, so she gets the self-employed thing. Then Frank, eventually, because I'd want to buy from his firm, not fight it. Burning bridges in this trade is stupid.

say: I'd say AI is a **good tool**, nothing more, and the hype was **sales talk**.
I'd say builders just want the **timber on Tuesday**.
think: Being **ahead on the tools** helps me while the field stays level.
A slowdown in **house building** matters more to me than AI.
do: Use AI to avoid repeats of the **decking mistake**.
Grow the **offcuts business** to about six hundred a month.
Start saving for a **van** for my own trade supply business.
feel: **Calm**, and a bit **fired up** to build something.
S0.quote: Builders don't care how I find the price, they just want the timber on Tuesday.
fieldNote: His ambition is **his own business**, rooted in his granddad's advice.
He reads risk through **house-building demand**, not AI.
He'd keep Frank (his boss) as a **supplier**, not a rival.

steps.text: Use AI price tracking to avoid another decking overstock
Grow the online offcuts business to six hundred a month
Save towards a delivery van for his own business

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say adapt or get left behind, and I'd say it to anyone who'd listen. It's not the government's job to protect every role. Firms that use it well will win, and so will the people who learn it fastest.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think the buying team at work shrinks to one or two, and Frank's the obvious one to stay. I'm junior, so I might be out. But I already run half my day through these tools, so I'm also the one who can set the system up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First, I'd offer to set up the AI ordering for the whole timber range, to make myself useful. Second, I'd speed up my own business plan, aiming to start part-time with a hired van within a year. And I'd use the same AI tools to run it, quotes, orders, invoices, so it's just me and a driver.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but more excited than scared. Change like this is when small guys get a chance.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said it's not the government's job. What if a friend lost their job?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then family and friends help, like they always have. My cousin lost his job at a print shop and my uncle took him on. I'd do the same, give someone a few days driving for me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there a risk you're not seeing?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably that every laid-off buyer has the same idea as me. If ten little suppliers pop up in my town, there's not enough work for all of us. That's why I'd move in the first year, not the third.

I'd say it's **not the government's job** to protect every role.

Start my own **trade supply business** part-time with a hired van within a year.
Run the new business on **AI tools** so it's just me and a driver.
S1.quote: Change like this is when small guys get a chance.
fieldNote: He sees disruption as **opportunity** for small firms.
His **traditional view** shows in relying on family over government.
He spots the **crowding risk** of many laid-off buyers starting firms.

steps.text: Set up AI ordering for the distributor's timber range
Start a part-time trade supply business with a hired van
Lean on family to share driving work if needed

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a shock, but people have to get on with it, no point crying. I'd say the government should get out of the way and let businesses adjust. At work I'd say we've got two years, let's move.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think my buying job is gone by 2028, and frankly Frank's too. But builders still need materials on site, and delivery and loading are hands-on until about 2031. So a small supplier with a van has three years of real work, maybe more.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd quit within six months and put my savings plus the offcuts money into a second-hand van and a small yard. I'd use AI for all the office side from day one. Lucia would keep her salon job, which is hands-on too, so we'd have her wage while I get going.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, honestly, more than I'd admit to my mates. It's a big bet with three months of savings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Three months of savings and a new business. Is that enough?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, not really. I'd need a loan, and I'd ask my uncle before a bank. If it goes wrong, I'm twenty-nine with debt and no job, which is the bit that keeps me up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens in 2031, when the robots arrive?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then the van drives itself, I suppose, and I'm a business owner with machines instead of a worker without one. That's the bet. Better to own the robot than to be replaced by it.

I'd say the **government** should get out of the way and let businesses adjust.
think: My buying job is gone by **2028**, and Frank's too.

fieldNote: He'd **bet everything** on his own firm, timed to the robot gap.

steps.text: Quit the buyer job within six months

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is plenty for anyone with a bit of get-up-and-go. I'd tell my mates to stop moaning and start planning. At work I'd keep my head down and learn everything I can from Frank.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think the buying job goes around 2031, but by then I'd have my own business running for a couple of years. Delivery robots come around 2034, so I'd have time to buy them myself if they're any good. Five years is about right for me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stay at work two more years, soaking up Frank's contacts and how he reads builders. Meanwhile I'd grow the offcuts business into a proper weekend supplier. Then around 2029 I'd go full-time on my own, with a van, a yard and AI doing the paperwork.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but in a good way. It's like the start of a race.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you need to have saved by 2029?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: About fifteen thousand for the van and the first stock. Lucia and I would cut the holidays and eat in. It's two years of being boring, and then we'd see.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you and Lucia change any family plans?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd wait on kids until the business is on its feet, maybe 2031. My granddad the carpenter always said to start your workshop before you marry, and that's the right order.

I'd tell mates to **stop moaning** and start planning.

fieldNote: The five-year gap fits his **business timeline** neatly.

He'd **delay children** until the business stands, echoing his granddad.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is loads of time, and anyone who's surprised in 2036 wasn't paying attention. I'd be fairly upbeat about it. At work I'd just get on with the job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think this is the best one for me. I'd have time to learn the trade properly, build the business slowly and buy the machines when they're cheap. By 2039, when the robots come, I'd want to be the one owning them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stay at the distributor three or four years and try to get promoted. I'd build the weekend business and buy a van outright, no loan. Then I'd go full-time around 2031 with a few regular builders already signed up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. It's a long runway, and I like long runways.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything that could go wrong?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A housing crash worries me more than AI, because if nobody's building, nobody needs timber. I'd keep the business small and debt-free so a bad year doesn't sink it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Frank about it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell him straight, once I'm ready, and ask if he'd supply me. He's nearly sixty, so maybe he'd even want to sell me some of his small accounts. Better that than they go to a big chain.

I'd be **upbeat** and just get on with the job.

By 2039 I'd want to be the one **owning the robots**.

Build the weekend business and buy a **van outright**, no loan.

S4.quote: A housing crash worries me more than AI, because if nobody's building, nobody needs timber.
fieldNote: The ten-year picture suits his **slow-build plan** best.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because I'd be betting everything on three months of savings with no time to build up. What would help is cheap start-up loans and less red tape for small firms, so people can start something instead of waiting for help.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask who owns the machines. Everyone asks who loses their job, but nobody asks who'll own the AI and the robots. I want ordinary people like me owning some of it, not just the big firms.

headlineQuote: Everyone asks who loses their job, but nobody asks who'll own the AI and the robots.
portrait: Zane is a **27-year-old junior buyer** of timber and sheet materials, living with Lucia, a hairdresser.
He uses **AI tools daily** and sells offcuts online, about three hundred a month.
Inspired by his carpenter **granddad**, he wants his own trade supply business.
His **traditional, free-market** view favours family help and less red tape over government support.
He stays **calm to anxious**, treating each scenario as a timeline for launching his firm.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because he'd bet everything on three months of savings.
whatWouldHelp: Cheap **start-up loans** and less **red tape** for small firms.
